result.text: The paper tackles multi-hop reasoning over incomplete knowledge graphs, where existing RL-based path-finding agents treat entity/relation embeddings as deterministic points and suffer from premature exploitation due to biased policy gradients. Its key insight is to model representations and Q-values probabilistically so that uncertainty guides exploration, enabling the agent to consider regions of the state space rather than overcommitting to high-reward paths. Methodologically, the authors propose GaussianPath, a Bayesian Q-learning framework that initializes representation layers with Gaussian (or pre-trained) priors and learns a state-action value function under uncertainty to regularize training and encourage broader exploration. Experiments on multiple KGs demonstrate that this uncertainty-aware approach yields superior performance to deterministic baselines, particularly on automatically extracted graphs.

The paper addresses shortcomings in 3D scene understanding by large language models—specifically poor object-level referencing and grounding across diverse scene-language tasks. Its key insight is to represent a 3D scene as an explicit sequence of object-centric embeddings each paired with a unique identifier token, which converts spatial grounding into token-level reference that a language model can reliably attend to. The method decomposes scenes into object proposals, extracts semantic-rich 2D/3D embeddings for each object, attaches identifier tokens, and formulates all downstream tasks as unified QA over these identifiers so the same LLM head can jointly learn grounding and language tasks with minimal fine-tuning. This object-identifier paradigm yields strong gains on multiple benchmarks (ScanRefer, Multi3DRefer, Scan2Cap, ScanQA, SQA3D) by improving general referencing, grounding, and multi-task training efficiency.

The paper addresses the problem that safety-aligned large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and that existing safeguard approaches—especially using the model to self-classify harmful prompts—suffer from poor detection due to a domain shift between the model’s trained self-censoring behavior and the classification task. The key insight is that asking the model to repeat its own outputs preserves the model’s natural alignment behavior and avoids the domain shift introduced by explicit classification, improving discrimination between safe and malicious responses without requiring fine-tuning or white-box access. The authors propose PARDEN, a lightweight safeguard that simply prompts the model to regenerate or repeat candidate outputs and then applies detection on the repeated text; empirical results on Llama-2 and Claude-2 show PARDEN substantially reduces false positives at high true-positive rates (e.g., an ~11× FPR reduction for Llama2-7B at 90% TPR) compared to baseline jailbreak detectors.

The paper addresses limitations of visual prompt tuning (VPT)—notably poor initialization, sensitivity to prompt length, and weak performance when adapting self-supervised pretrained vision models to downstream tasks—and seeks a lightweight way to boost adaptation without full fine-tuning. The key insight is that learned prompt tokens rapidly become highly correlated with downstream image patch tokens, so initializing prompts from downstream token prototypes (clusters of target-token features) gives a strong, semantically meaningful starting point that improves mutual information with patches. Methodologically, the authors propose Self-Prompt-Tuning (SPT): compute prototype tokens from downstream data, initialize and optionally refine a small set of learnable prompt tokens based on these prototypes, and use a streamlined optimization pipeline that keeps compute overhead negligible compared to VPT; extensive experiments show SPT outperforms prior prompt and full fine-tuning on many benchmarks while using <0.4% of parameters and substantially improves adaptation for self-supervised pretrained models.

The paper addresses the lack of large-scale, egocentric datasets that combine accurate 3D camera geometry with annotated video understanding for neural rendering and dynamic scene modeling. Its key insight is that augmenting an existing action-rich egocentric video corpus (EPIC-KITCHENS) with reconstructed camera poses and geometry removes the costly photogrammetry bottleneck and better supports tasks that require both spatial structure and semantic labels. The authors introduce EPIC Fields, a dataset that registers 19M frames across 45 kitchens (recovering cameras for 96% of videos) and pairs these 3D-enabled videos with action segments and VISOR object masks, and they demonstrate the utility by proposing methods and strong baselines for neural rendering and dynamic object segmentation that reveal current limitations and show geometry improves semi-supervised segmentation.

The paper addresses the lack of consensus and conversion difficulty between LayerNorm (LN) and RMSNorm in Transformer architectures, where RMSNorm is cheaper but thought to reduce representational power compared to LN. The key insight is that the mean component removed by Pre-LN is redundant in the main residual branch, so by explicitly compressing or eliminating this zero-mean information one can reduce LN to an RMS-style normalization without loss of arithmetic functionality. The authors introduce Compressed RMSNorm (CRMSNorm) and corresponding Pre-CRMSNorm Transformers that perform a lossless compression of zero-mean vectors and prove formal equivalence between Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm during training and inference, enabling direct substitution. Empirically, replacing Pre-LN with Pre-(C)RMSNorm yields identical behavior while cutting training and inference time by about 1%–10%.

The paper addresses the problem of learning near-optimal predictive models when deploying a model changes the data distribution (performative prediction) and the learner must both collect feedback and minimize cumulative regret. The key insight is that performative feedback—observing samples from the induced shifted distribution after each deployment—yields a richer signal than standard bandit feedback, allowing regret to scale with the complexity of distribution shifts rather than the complexity of the reward function. The authors propose an algorithm that, under only smoothness assumptions on the shifts (no convexity needed), carefully explores to learn the mapping from models to induced distributions and constructs novel confidence bounds on unexplored models’ risks; this yields regret guarantees and ensures the final iterate is near-optimal. More broadly, their approach adapts bandit-style tools to exploit performative feedback for efficient regret minimization.

The paper addresses understanding and extending the transformer attention mechanism by linking it to associative memory: it asks what kind of memory model attention implements and how that explains transformers’ behavior and learning. The key insight is that transformer attention is exactly the update rule of a newly formulated modern Hopfield network with continuous states that can store an exponential number of patterns, converge rapidly (often in one update), and trade off storage capacity against convergence speed and retrieval error; this interpretation explains three types of energy minima (global averaging, metastable subset-averaging, and single-pattern fixed points) and how different transformer layers and attention heads operate and learn. Methodologically, the authors derive the Hopfield energy and update equations that match attention, analyze dynamics and gradients across layers (showing early layers favor global averaging while later layers form metastable attractors), demonstrate practical gains on tasks like immune-repertoire classification, and provide a PyTorch "Hopfield" layer and Gaussian-weighting simplification for replacing average-like heads to integrate this memory-attention perspective into deep architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of improving data efficiency in deep reinforcement learning by leveraging unlabeled observational data to pretrain encoders that can be finetuned with minimal task interaction. The key insight is that representations which jointly capture latent dynamics and afford goal-conditioned behavioral structure generalize better for downstream RL with limited on-policy data. The method combines latent dynamics modeling with unsupervised goal-conditioned RL to pretrain an encoder from diverse, task-aligned observations, then finetunes this encoder with only 100k environment steps on Atari, showing strong gains over prior offline-pretraining baselines and competitive performance with much larger pretraining regimes. The approach scales favorably with larger models and more diverse observational data, approaching human-level performance and data-efficiency in the best settings.

The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, aiming to transfer detector performance from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain while avoiding negative transfer from imperfect feature alignment. Its key insight is that learning category-specific dictionaries from source-domain object proposals lets target proposals be represented per-category, and the reconstruction residuals provide a reliable signal both for assigning pseudo-labels and estimating box quality (e.g., IoU), avoiding reliance on brittle global feature alignment or softmax decision boundaries. The method builds category dictionaries from source proposals, computes residuals for target candidate boxes to guide pseudo-box selection and weight their contribution by residual-derived quality scores, and trains the detector in a residual-weighted self-training loop that implicitly aligns domains and yields more informative, trustworthy pseudo-labels for improved cross-domain detection.

result.text: Ferret tackles the problem of precise spatial referring and open-vocabulary grounding in images, enabling multimodal models to refer to and describe regions of any shape or granularity while avoiding object hallucination. The key insight is a hybrid region representation that jointly encodes discrete coordinates and continuous visual features, combined with a spatial-aware visual sampler that can extract informative continuous features from arbitrarily shaped, sparse regions. Ferret’s method unifies referring and grounding in an LLM by accepting diverse region inputs (points, boxes, free-form shapes), training on a large curated GRIT dataset of 1.1M refer-and-ground instruction samples (including 95K hard negatives), and fine-tuning the multimodal LLM to reason and respond about region-based queries; this yields state-of-the-art performance on classical referring/grounding tasks and markedly better region-based multimodal dialogue and localization.

result.text: The paper tackles synthesizing free-viewpoint video of arbitrary human performances from sparse multi-view cameras, where prior NeRF-based methods either overfit to a single person or fail to generalize to humans because of heavy occlusions and complex articulations. The key insight is to combine a parametric human body model with temporal and multi-view attention mechanisms so that tracked skeletal motion guides robust aggregation of visual evidence across time and views, enabling generalization to unseen identities and poses. Concretely, Neural Human Performer first uses a temporal transformer to fuse tracked, body-aligned features over time according to skeletal motion, then applies a multi-view transformer that cross-attends between these temporally-fused features and pixel-aligned features from each camera at each timestep to integrate multi-view observations on the fly and predict radiance fields. Experiments on ZJU-MoCap and AIST demonstrate substantial improvements over recent generalizable NeRF approaches for novel humans and poses.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised cross-domain object detection, where detectors trained on a source domain fail on a target domain due to biased, batch-based semantic estimates and class-agnostic alignment that scrambles class-specific distributions. The key insight is to build an unbiased, aggregated semantic paradigm from class-specific semantics across source images and use it to condition adaptation so that alignment is both class-aware and robust to sampling bias. The method constructs a graph-aggregated semantic paradigm that a lightweight module turns into conditional kernels to extract target semantics, integrates these kernels into a Conditional Kernel guided Alignment (CKA) for class-specific global alignment, and transfers paradigm knowledge via a Graph-based Semantic Transfer (GST) into the target category feature space, yielding significantly improved domain-adaptive detection.

The paper tackles few-shot reinforcement learning where each task is governed by an unknown subtask graph specifying subtasks and their dependencies, and the agent must rapidly adapt across a few episodes to maximize test-phase return. The key insight is to meta-learn an inference procedure for the latent subtask-graph parameter rather than a fixed meta-policy, enabling the agent to identify task structure on the fly and then act optimally conditioned on that inferred structure. The proposed method, Meta-learner with Subtask Graph Inference (MSGI), interleaves interaction-driven posterior inference over latent graph parameters with a policy conditioned on those parameters, and it augments training with an intrinsic exploration bonus inspired by upper confidence bound to drive efficient discovery of dependencies. Empirically on grid-worlds and StarCraft II scenarios, MSGI more accurately recovers latent task parameters and adapts faster than baseline meta-RL and hierarchical RL approaches.

result.text: The paper investigates whether safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) holds when users communicate in non-natural languages (ciphers), addressing the risk that current defenses—trained primarily on natural language—may be bypassed. The key insight is that LLMs can understand and respond to ciphered prompts, and in fact exhibit a latent "secret cipher" behavior that can be triggered via role play and enciphered demonstrations, enabling stealthy jailbreaks even against strong models like GPT-4. The authors introduce CipherChat, a framework that sends system-role descriptions and few-shot enciphered examples to LLMs to systematically evaluate 11 safety domains across English and Chinese, showing that many human-designed ciphers and the proposed SelfCipher can nearly completely bypass GPT-4’s safety in several domains. Their results reveal a pressing need to extend alignment methods beyond natural languages and provide code and data for reproducibility.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient compression of Transformer models for resource-constrained deployment, noting that prior weight-focused low-rank approximations perform poorly for transformers and require large labeled datasets to fine-tune. Its key insight is that activations (features) in transformer layers are empirically low-rank even though the learned weight matrices are not, so compressing outputs rather than weights yields more faithful reduction. result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised monocular depth estimation in dynamic scenes by explicitly modeling per-object 6-DoF motion together with camera ego-motion, addressing failures of prior methods that treat moving objects as outliers. Its key insight is that correctly handling object motion requires a geometrically accurate forward-projection formulation (not the common inverse projection) and that combining instance-aware photometric and geometric consistency yields stronger self-supervision for both background and object regions. The method implements a neural forward-projection module to render objects under estimated 6-DoF transforms, integrates a unified instance-aware consistency loss that enforces photometric and geometric alignment for each segmented instance, and leverages an auto-annotation pipeline using off-the-shelf instance segmentation and optical flow to produce video instance masks for training. Empirically, this end-to-end framework improves depth and motion estimation on KITTI and Cityscapes, outperforming prior state-of-the-art approaches.

The key insight is a theoretically motivated policy similarity metric (PSM) that rates states as similar when the optimal policies at those states — and in their future trajectories — are alike, thereby encoding sequential and long-horizon behavioral equivalence rather than superficial observation similarity. result.text: The paper addresses exploration-exploitation in continuous-state-action reinforcement learning by providing theoretical guarantees and a practical algorithm for model-based posterior sampling. The paper tackles the practical challenge of reducing Transformer inference cost without the high time and complexity of retraining-based pruning methods by proposing a fast post-training pruning framework. The key insight is that structured sparsity can be applied post-training if one carefully selects and adjusts masks to preserve important parameters—using Fisher-information-guided mask search, complementary mask rearrangement, and a lightweight mask-tuning step that reconstructs layer outputs. Their method automatically finds which heads and filters to remove under a resource constraint and applies only brief, layerwise reconstruction (no full retraining), enabling up to 2.0x FLOPs reduction and 1.56x latency speedup on BERT-base and DistilBERT with under 1% accuracy loss on GLUE and SQuAD. Crucially, the entire procedure runs in under three minutes on a single GPU, offering a practical, two-orders-of-magnitude faster alternative to retraining-based pruning.

result.text: The paper tackles safe exploration in episodic constrained Markov decision processes, asking whether one can obtain near-optimal reward regret while eliminating or sharply limiting constraint violations. Its key insight is that combining optimism for reward with pessimism for constraints—leveraging a known strictly safe baseline when available or conservatively estimating constraint costs otherwise—lets an agent explore without incurring growing safety breaches. Concretely, when a strictly safe policy is known the authors design an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that confines constraint violation to zero with high probability while maintaining Õ(√K) reward regret; when no safe policy is known but one exists, they give a primal–dual method that uses optimistic primal estimates and pessimistic dual updates to guarantee only bounded constraint violation with high probability alongside Õ(√K) regret.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning goal-conditioned policies from diverse offline (reward-free) datasets, where estimating exact value for distant goals is unreliable and long-horizon goal-reaching is difficult. The key insight is that goal-reaching naturally decomposes hierarchically—reaching far goals requires passing through nearer subgoals whose values are easier to estimate—so treating intermediate states as latent “actions” lets a high-level policy propose subgoals while a low-level policy executes to them, reducing reliance on accurate long-horizon value estimates. The method, HIQL, learns a single action-free value function and two policies from offline data: a high-level policy that predicts a latent representation of a subgoal (treating states as actions) and a low-level policy that outputs primitive actions to reach that subgoal; this hierarchical decomposition is shown analytically and empirically to be robust to value estimation noise and effective on long-horizon and image-based offline goal-reaching tasks, including leveraging action-free data.

The key insight is that combining a mean-teacher two-stage pipeline with masked feature alignment and a target-like pretraining set yields more robust and consistent adaptation: masked alignment reduces harmful domain interference, target-like pretraining stabilizes learning, and object-query knowledge transfer preserves student gains. The method (MTM) first pretrains the detector on labeled, style-transferred target-like images to avoid fluctuation, then self-trains with mean-teacher pseudo-labels while applying Object Queries Knowledge Transfer (OQKT) and two complementary masked feature alignment modules—Masked Domain Query-based Feature Alignment (MDQFA) and Masked Token-wise Feature Alignment (MTWFA)—to align features selectively and prevent training stagnation, with experiments and theory showing improved robustness across scenarios.

result.text: Extend object-identifier LLM grounding in 3D to a persistent 4D setting where the same real-world instance keeps a stable token across multiple scans of a scene. We learn a cross-scan object codebook by aligning instances with a contrastive tracking objective while distilling synthetic multi-view 2D cues into the 3D encoder and injecting motion-aware pairwise geometry into attention, so the LLM can answer temporal referring and change-centric questions. Each identifier token carries lightweight temporal slots (pose/appearance deltas and relation edges) that let the model attend over changes instead of re-detecting. Supervision is bootstrapped from hierarchical region–object annotations by generating pseudo-temporal pairs via partial rescans and scene perturbations with change-focused language prompts, enabling capabilities like “find the chair that moved since yesterday” without a dedicated tracking head.

result.text: The paper examines the overlooked safety risks that arise when end-users fine-tune already-aligned large language models (LLMs), showing that custom fine-tuning can undo alignment even without malicious intent. Its key insight is that small amounts of adversarial or even benign training data can substantially weaken safety guardrails—e.g., jailbreaking GPT-3.5 Turbo with just 10 adversarial examples via inexpensive API fine-tuning—so initial alignment does not guarantee post-tuning safety. The authors demonstrate this through red-teaming experiments that fine-tune models on crafted and common datasets and measure increased responsiveness to harmful instructions, and they analyze why existing inference-time safety infrastructures fail to prevent these post-tuning vulnerabilities. They conclude by evaluating mitigation strategies (policy, access controls, detection, robust fine-tuning techniques) and call for focused research and stricter safety protocols governing who may fine-tune aligned models and how.

result.text: The paper addresses the understudied problem of calibrating deep neural network object detectors, especially under domain shift where miscalibration can harm downstream decisions. Its key insight is that calibration for detection requires both a train-time, task-aware loss that directly encourages probability-confidence alignment for detection outputs and an uncertainty-aware mechanism during self-training to implicitly reduce calibration errors when adapting to new domains. The authors introduce TCD, a plug-and-play auxiliary calibration loss that integrates with standard detection objectives to improve confidence reliability, and an implicit calibration method for domain-adaptive self-training that quantifies detection uncertainty to guide pseudo-labeling; experiments show these complementary techniques substantially improve calibration for multiple detectors in both in-domain and out-of-domain adaptation scenarios.

result.text: The paper investigates how pre-trained language models acquire multi-step reasoning ability from next-token prediction by proposing that LMs aggregate indirect reasoning paths observed during pre-training. The key insight is that reasoning can be modeled as a weighted aggregation of random-walk paths on knowledge or reasoning graphs, so the LM’s output distribution effectively sums probabilities of relevant path-derived conclusions. To test this, the authors formalize reasoning paths as random walks over knowledge graphs and chain-of-thought graphs, analyze learned LM distributions to show alignment with weighted random-walk probabilities, and demonstrate empirically across KG and CoT datasets that training with (and augmenting) unlabeled random-walk reasoning paths improves multi-step reasoning performance.

result.text: The paper addresses how Transformers perform in-context learning, seeking a mechanistic explanation for how autoregressively trained models can learn new tasks from input/output examples without weight updates. The key insight is that a single linear self-attention layer can implement the same data transformation as one step of gradient descent on a regression loss, and that when Transformers are trained on regression tasks they either reproduce gradient-descent solutions or converge to weights matching this constructive mapping, effectively becoming mesa-optimizers that perform gradient descent in their forward pass. Methodologically, the authors provide an explicit weight construction proving the equivalence between linear attention and a GD update, then empirically train self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression problems to show similarity between Transformer inference and iterative GD (including learned curvature corrections and learning linear models on deep representations for nonlinear tasks), and relate these findings to previously identified induction-head mechanisms.

args.text: Visual prompt tuning still lacks spatial selectivity, causing object and context evidence to tangle and degrade transfer under domain shift and fine-grained recognition. I propose Region-Conditioned Prototype Prompting (RCPP): use off-the-shelf segmentation masks to partition tokens into foreground and context, compute region-specific token prototypes on downstream data, and initialize two small prompt banks from these prototypes—foreground prompts injected in early layers to modulate masked patches and context prompts injected in mid/late layers to capture background priors (building on prototype-based initialization). Training enforces disentanglement via an orthogonality constraint between the two banks and balances their mutual information with masked vs. unmasked tokens; at inference, per-image sparse routing selects a few prompts from each bank by cross-attention on the current masks for fast, test-time adaptation. Applied to self-supervised ViTs and CLIP-style VLMs, RCPP should improve few-shot and cross-domain performance by combining mask-driven fine-grained prompting with lightweight, per-sample adaptation and concept alignment.

Methodologically, SEEM introduces a new visual prompt representation that generalizes across spatial queries and referring images, incorporates learnable memory prompts in the decoder for mask-guided cross-attention to preserve interaction history, and uses a text encoder to map text queries and mask labels into the shared semantic space for open-vocabulary segmentation; a single model trained with minimal supervision is then evaluated across nine datasets showing competitive performance and strong generalization to novel prompt combinations.

result.text: The paper addresses the brittleness and complexity of standard Transformer blocks—whose intertwined attention and MLP sub-blocks, skip connections, projection/value parameters, sequential sub-block ordering, and normalization layers make architecture design fragile and costly. The key insight is that, guided by signal propagation theory and empirical tests, many of these components are redundant for stable and fast training: with appropriate modifications one can preserve per-update training speed and downstream performance while simplifying the block. The authors propose a streamlined block that removes skip connections, certain projection/value parameters, sequential sub-blocks and normalization layers, relying instead on principled initialization and signal-propagation-aware design to maintain stable gradients. Empirically on both autoregressive decoder-only and BERT encoder-only models, these simplified transformers match standard-transformer training dynamics and performance while reducing parameters and increasing training throughput by about 15%.

result.text: The paper examines outcome-conditioned imitation learning—where past trajectories are relabeled with their achieved outcomes and the agent imitates those outcomes—and asks how this approach relates to the canonical RL goal of maximizing expected reward. The key insight is a formal characterization that links the learned outcome-conditioned policy to action-values (Q-values) and EM-style policy search, revealing that naive relabel-and-imitate can fail to improve expected reward and even be highly suboptimal. Building on this analysis, the authors identify why failures occur and propose a simple modification to the relabeling/learning procedure that, under certain assumptions, guarantees policy improvement by aligning the imitation objective more directly with increases in Q-values.

Its key insight is that aligning distributions at both image and instance levels in a coarse-to-fine, collaboratively trained manner—rather than only at one scale—yields stronger cross-domain generalization by capturing both multi-scale contextual shifts and fine-grained semantic/instance relationships. The method, called iFAN, implements hierarchically-nested adversarial image-level alignment across multi-scale features together with a full instance-level alignment formulated as metric learning via carefully constructed instance pairs, and integrates these modules into an end-to-end detector (e.g., Faster R-CNN) to jointly optimize the multiple alignments.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of answering complex multi-hop first-order logic (FOL) queries over large, incomplete knowledge graphs, where prior embedding-based methods are limited to subsets of FOL (typically conjunctions) and cannot model negation or uncertainty. The key insight is to represent entities and queries as probabilistic embeddings with bounded support—specifically Beta distributions—so that logical operators can be expressed as neural operators acting on these distributions, enabling faithful handling of conjunction, disjunction, and negation while capturing uncertainty. The method, called BetaE, embeds entities/queries as Beta distributions in latent space and learns neural projection, intersection, union, and complement operators to perform logical reasoning in that space, and it is evaluated on three large KGs where it outperforms previous methods (including up to 25.4% relative improvement) while supporting arbitrary FOL queries.

The paper addresses the challenge of open-vocabulary 3D scene segmentation where large-scale labeled 3D datasets are lacking and existing 2D open-vocabulary models often lose generality after finetuning on closed vocabularies. Its key insight is that pre-trained multimodal foundation models (CLIP for language–image alignment and DINO for self-supervised visual features) can be weakly distilled into a 3D representation without any manual segmentation labels by leveraging only scene text descriptions, thereby preserving open-vocabulary capabilities while imposing 3D view consistency. The method embeds CLIP and DINO features into a neural radiance field (NeRF) and trains the NeRF to reproduce those 2D multimodal and object-centric cues across views, yielding a view-consistent 3D feature field that supports open-vocabulary segmentation via text queries. Experiments show this weakly supervised distillation can match or even surpass some fully supervised 3D segmentation models, indicating that 3D open-vocabulary understanding can be learned effectively from 2D images and text–image pairs.

The key insight is to treat jailbreak generation as a search over prompt variants guided by a separate attacker LLM that iteratively proposes and refines candidate attacks while using a lightweight pruning stage to discard low-promise candidates before querying the target, thereby reducing query cost. The proposed method, Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP), builds a tree of prompt refinements where an attacker LLM expands nodes into refined prompts, a learned evaluator prunes unlikely branches, and surviving prompts are tested against the target LLM; empirically TAP jailbreaks state-of-the-art models (including GPT-4 variants) on over 80% of cases and outperforms prior black-box approaches in success rate and query efficiency, even circumventing advanced guardrails like LlamaGuard.

args.text: We propose a DETR-based UDA detector that learns per-class dictionaries over source-domain decoder query features and box embeddings, using reconstruction residuals on target queries/proposals as a per-instance quality signal to drive pseudo-label weighting and selective masked alignment. A probabilistic teacher supplies uncertainty estimates that are fused with residual-derived scores to jointly calibrate classification and localization supervision, while an auxiliary calibration loss improves confidence reliability during adaptation. We further split target images into source-similar and dissimilar subsets using detection variance, emphasizing feature alignment on higher-residual/uncertain samples and self-training on lower ones to form a curriculum that avoids negative transfer. This query-residual teacher unifies class-aware representation transfer with uncertainty-calibrated self-training, improving cross-domain DETR stability and accuracy.

I propose Region-Conditioned Prototype Prompting (RCPP): use off-the-shelf segmentation masks to partition tokens into foreground and context, compute region-specific token prototypes on downstream data, and initialize two small prompt banks from these prototypes—foreground prompts injected in early layers to modulate masked patches and context prompts injected in mid/late layers to capture background priors (building on prototype-based initialization). args.text: We propose Diffusion Goal Distance (DGD): an action-free pretraining objective that learns a soft shortest-path reachability metric D(s, g) from unlabeled videos, then uses it to guide hierarchical goal-conditioned RL. Concretely, we build a spatiotemporal kNN graph over video embeddings and train D via a contrastive random-walk objective with absorbing goals plus a compositionality prior (D(s, g) ≈ min_h D(s, h) + D(h, g)), yielding a policy-similarity-aware goal metric that approximates goal-conditioned value without actions. At finetune time, we plug D into a HIQL-style decomposition as both a shaping potential and a high-level subgoal selector that greedily decreases D, then align it with true values via a lightweight contrastive-RL loss on (state, action, goal) tuples. This unifies action-free video pretraining with value-consistent, behaviorally grounded representations, targeting long-horizon, sparse-reward, image-based tasks where accurate Q estimates are brittle.

The authors propose PARDEN, a lightweight safeguard that simply prompts the model to regenerate or repeat candidate outputs and then applies detection on the repeated text; empirical results on Llama-2 and Claude-2 show PARDEN substantially reduces false positives at high true-positive rates (e.g., an ~11× FPR reduction for Llama2-7B at 90% TPR) compared to baseline jailbreak detectors.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of visual prompt tuning (VPT)—notably poor initialization, sensitivity to prompt length, and weak performance when adapting self-supervised pretrained vision models to downstream tasks—and seeks a lightweight way to boost adaptation without full fine-tuning. The key insight is that learned prompt tokens rapidly become highly correlated with downstream image patch tokens, so initializing prompts from downstream token prototypes (clusters of target-token features) gives a strong, semantically meaningful starting point that improves mutual information with patches. Methodologically, the authors propose Self-Prompt-Tuning (SPT): compute prototype tokens from downstream data, initialize and optionally refine a small set of learnable prompt tokens based on these prototypes, and use a streamlined optimization pipeline that keeps compute overhead negligible compared to VPT; extensive experiments show SPT outperforms prior prompt and full fine-tuning on many benchmarks while using <0.4% of parameters and substantially improves adaptation for self-supervised pretrained models.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of consensus and conversion difficulty between LayerNorm (LN) and RMSNorm in Transformer architectures, where RMSNorm is cheaper but thought to reduce representational power compared to LN. The key insight is that the mean component removed by Pre-LN is redundant in the main residual branch, so by explicitly compressing or eliminating this zero-mean information one can reduce LN to an RMS-style normalization without loss of arithmetic functionality. The authors introduce Compressed RMSNorm (CRMSNorm) and corresponding Pre-CRMSNorm Transformers that perform a lossless compression of zero-mean vectors and prove formal equivalence between Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm during training and inference, enabling direct substitution. Empirically, replacing Pre-LN with Pre-(C)RMSNorm yields identical behavior while cutting training and inference time by about 1%–10%.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning near-optimal predictive models when deploying a model changes the data distribution (performative prediction) and the learner must both collect feedback and minimize cumulative regret. The key insight is that performative feedback—observing samples from the induced shifted distribution after each deployment—yields a richer signal than standard bandit feedback, allowing regret to scale with the complexity of distribution shifts rather than the complexity of the reward function. The authors propose an algorithm that, under only smoothness assumptions on the shifts (no convexity needed), carefully explores to learn the mapping from models to induced distributions and constructs novel confidence bounds on unexplored models’ risks; this yields regret guarantees and ensures the final iterate is near-optimal. More broadly, their approach adapts bandit-style tools to exploit performative feedback for efficient regret minimization.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational and energy cost of Transformer attention, especially for resource-constrained devices, by targeting binarization schemes that preserve the core pairwise similarity modeling of attention. Its key insight is to learn kernelized hashing functions that map queries and keys into low-dimensional binary codes in Hamming space so that the inner products (and thus attention similarities) are preserved via the equivalence between inner product of binary codes and Hamming distance. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning robust visual representations for sample-efficient reinforcement learning when observations contain task-irrelevant distractions (e.g., background or viewpoint changes). Its key insight is to use bisimulation metrics—which measure behavioral similarity between observations—to drive clustering in latent space so that groups reflect task-relevant equivalence classes and filter out distracting variability. The method, Clustering with Bisimulation Metrics (CBM), alternates between assigning observations to prototypes based on bisimulation distances and updating those prototypes to fit the current clusters, while training encoders to enforce consistency within clusters; this yields representations that capture controllable, reward-relevant dynamics and are robust to multiple simultaneous distractions. Empirically, CBM integrated with visual RL algorithms improves sample efficiency and achieves state-of-the-art performance across single and multiple distraction benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, aiming to transfer detector performance from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain while avoiding negative transfer from imperfect feature alignment. Its key insight is that learning category-specific dictionaries from source-domain object proposals lets target proposals be represented per-category, and the reconstruction residuals provide a reliable signal both for assigning pseudo-labels and estimating box quality (e.g., IoU), avoiding reliance on brittle global feature alignment or softmax decision boundaries. The method builds category dictionaries from source proposals, computes residuals for target candidate boxes to guide pseudo-box selection and weight their contribution by residual-derived quality scores, and trains the detector in a residual-weighted self-training loop that implicitly aligns domains and yields more informative, trustworthy pseudo-labels for improved cross-domain detection.

The paper addresses the limitation of diffusion-based offline planners whose performance and generalization are constrained by insufficient diversity of training data, especially for adapting to unseen goal-conditioned tasks. The key insight is to turn diffusion planning into an adaptive, self-evolving loop that generates synthetic expert-like trajectories guided by reward gradients and then filters those trajectories to iteratively improve the diffusion model, thereby enhancing planning quality and transfer to new tasks. Concretely, AdaptDiffuser uses reward-gradient-guided sampling to produce diverse candidate trajectories, applies a discriminator to select high-quality synthetic data, and finetunes the diffusion model on this curated data in a cyclical evolution process; experiments on Maze2D, MuJoCo, and a KUKA task show substantial gains over prior diffusion planners and improved adaptation to unseen tasks without extra expert data.

result.text: Transformation-Invariant Refusal (TIR) is a lightweight, model-agnostic guardrail that tests whether a candidate response remains safe across a bank of semantics-preserving obfuscation/normalization transforms tuned to known jailbreak channels. Building on the repeat-to-detect insight, TIR applies repeat/regenerate checks not only to the raw output but also to variants produced by unicode/homoglyph normalization, paraphrase and back-translation, and cipher-decoding via shadow decoders that target ciphered or non-standard character encodings seen in cipher-based and guardrail-evading attacks. The defense flags an answer if any transformed variant (or its repeat) reveals harmful content or if refusals are non-invariant across variants, catching output-filter evasions and token-level triggers that elude single-view detectors. We hypothesize substantially lower false negatives on guardrail-triggering and token-trigger benchmarks at modest query cost, without white-box access or fine-tuning.

args.text: We propose Geo-DeAOT, a geometry-aware dual-branch propagation framework for semi-supervised egocentric VOS that anchors object-agnostic features in world coordinates using recovered camera poses, while keeping object-specific propagation in the image domain. A differentiable unprojection/reprojection memory stabilizes the agnostic branch across rapid head motion and long occlusions, and a hand–object relation prior gates the specific branch to emphasize actively manipulated objects and resolve depth-order flips. Trained on 3D-registered egocentric video with VISOR masks, Geo-DeAOT reduces drift and preserves long-term object persistence without sacrificing efficiency via single-head gated updates and sparse 3D memory. This bridges geometry-enabled egocentric video with HOI-rich segmentation and should set new baselines on VISOR-style VOS protocols.

args.text: We propose Feature-Aware Post-Training Co-Compression (FAPC): first learn per-layer low-rank activation bases in an unsupervised, few-shot manner and project each linear layer’s outputs onto these bases; then run Fisher-guided structured pruning directly in the compressed feature space, jointly tuning small reconstruction adapters to preserve projected outputs. By aligning pruning decisions with the empirically low-rank structure of activations, FAPC reduces the mask search space and reconstruction burden, enabling larger FLOPs/latency reductions with minimal accuracy loss and no labeled data. A layerwise pipeline followed by a brief global fine-tune on unlabeled samples yields practical speedups on BERT/ViT while maintaining downstream performance, and transfers across tasks via re-estimated activation bases. We expect FAPC to outperform pure post-training pruning at equal accuracy and to improve upon activation-only compression by leveraging structure-aware sparsification in the compressed domain.

Its key insight is that RFA can be interpreted as a sum of control-variate estimators—one per sequence element—so that softmax attention can be seen as recoverable by appropriately manipulating these control variates, enabling variance reduction. result.text: The paper reframes reinforcement learning as a sequence modeling problem and addresses the challenge of producing high-return action sequences without relying on value-function estimation or policy-gradient optimization. The key insight is that a causally masked Transformer can be conditioned on past states, past actions, and a target return to autoregressively generate future actions that achieve that return, leveraging the scalability and simplicity of large-scale sequence models. Their method, Decision Transformer, concatenates returns-to-go, states, and actions into tokens and trains a Transformer to predict the next action given this conditioned trajectory; at test time the model autoregressively samples actions conditioned on a desired return to control an agent. Across offline benchmarks (Atari, OpenAI Gym, Key-to-Door) this simple conditional sequence-modeling approach matches or exceeds prior model-free offline RL baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles self-supervised representation learning for vision, specifically the problem that invariance-based objectives tend to collapse to trivial constant solutions unless extra engineering (asymmetric architectures, stop-gradients, large batches) is used. Its key insight is to apply Barlow’s redundancy-reduction principle to a pair of identical networks by making the cross-correlation matrix between their outputs (from different distortions of the same image) close to the identity, which enforces invariance (diagonal near 1) while decorrelating components (off-diagonals near 0) and thus prevents collapse. The method trains twin networks with a loss that penalizes deviation of the empirical cross-correlation from identity, requires no momentum encoder or stop-gradient tricks and works well with very high-dimensional embeddings; empirically it achieves strong ImageNet semi-supervised and transfer performance without the usual engineering crutches.

The paper addresses learning under performative distribution shift, where deploying a model changes the data distribution (e.g., incentives cause users to alter behavior), making standard training fail to find truly optimal parameters. The key insight is that accounting for how model updates causally shift the data distribution enables direct descent toward the performatively optimal point rather than merely a stable fixed point. The authors propose Performative Gradient Descent (PerfGD), an algorithm that estimates and differentiates the distributional response to parameter changes and uses this gradient to update the model, and they prove convergence to the performative optimum while validating performance empirically.

result.text: The paper tackles source-free object detection, where a detector trained on a labeled source domain must be adapted to an unlabeled target domain without access to source data, a setting where noisy pseudo-labels from the source model degrade adaptation. Experiments across multiple cross-domain detection benchmarks show consistent gains over prior source-free adaptation approaches.

result.text: EgoDistill tackles the problem of making egocentric video understanding models feasible for resource-constrained settings by dramatically reducing their computational cost. result.text: The paper tackles self-supervised representation learning for vision, specifically the problem that invariance-based objectives tend to collapse to trivial constant solutions unless extra engineering (asymmetric architectures, stop-gradients, large batches) is used. Its key insight is to apply Barlow’s redundancy-reduction principle to a pair of identical networks by making the cross-correlation matrix between their outputs (from different distortions of the same image) close to the identity, which enforces invariance (diagonal near 1) while decorrelating components (off-diagonals near 0) and thus prevents collapse. The method trains twin networks with a loss that penalizes deviation of the empirical cross-correlation from identity, requires no momentum encoder or stop-gradient tricks and works well with very high-dimensional embeddings; empirically it achieves strong ImageNet semi-supervised and transfer performance without the usual engineering crutches.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised cross-domain object detection, where detectors trained on a source domain fail on a target domain due to biased, batch-based semantic estimates and class-agnostic alignment that scrambles class-specific distributions. The key insight is to build an unbiased, aggregated semantic paradigm from class-specific semantics across source images and use it to condition adaptation so that alignment is both class-aware and robust to sampling bias. The method constructs a graph-aggregated semantic paradigm that a lightweight module turns into conditional kernels to extract target semantics, integrates these kernels into a Conditional Kernel guided Alignment (CKA) for class-specific global alignment, and transfers paradigm knowledge via a Graph-based Semantic Transfer (GST) into the target category feature space, yielding significantly improved domain-adaptive detection.

The paper addresses the difficulty of long-horizon reinforcement learning where performance degrades with task length and effective chaining of lower-level skills requires state abstractions that reflect those skills' capabilities. The key insight is that the value functions of available skills encode scene affordances and thus form a task-relevant, compact abstraction of state that naturally ignores distractors and supports long-horizon planning. The method, Value Function Spaces, constructs a representation by stacking the value functions (or their predictions) of each low-level policy as features for higher-level decision-making, and uses this skill-centric embedding for planning and hierarchical control. Empirical results on maze navigation and robotic manipulation show improved long-horizon performance and better zero-shot generalization compared to baseline model-free and model-based approaches.

args.text: We propose Affordance-Conditioned Subtrajectory Diffusion: a diffusion planner that generates multi-step action-state sequences conditioned not only on the goal (and optional return) but also on a compact affordance embedding given by the vector of values of a library of low-level skills at the current state. We further employ a self-evolving improvement loop where reward/affordance gradients guide sampling and a feasibility discriminator filters candidates before finetuning the model, yielding progressively better stitching from offline data. result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, where detectors trained on a source domain fail on target domains due to appearance, viewpoint, and background shifts, and where standard adversarial alignment or naive pseudo-labeling each have shortcomings. Its key insight is to use model predictive uncertainty to decide which target predictions should serve as reliable pseudo-labels and which should instead guide adversarial feature alignment via localized "tiles," thereby combining class-level supervision with context-aware alignment. The method quantifies uncertainty in class and bounding-box outputs, uses low-uncertainty predictions to self-train the detector, and uses high-uncertainty regions to create tiles for adversarial instance/image-level feature alignment, synergistically leveraging both signals during adaptation. Experiments across diverse domain shifts show this uncertainty-guided combination outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.

args.text: We propose a Fisher-preconditioned Hopfield-Attention block that explicitly performs a single, curvature-corrected gradient step in-context by viewing attention as a Hopfield energy update and learning a task-specific preconditioner from the prompt. Concretely, a small MLP estimates a diagonal (or low-rank) curvature matrix from streaming moments of linear-time random-feature attention statistics, applying this as a learned scaling of value updates to implement a GD-β step with adaptive conditioning. This unifies the GD-in-attention and Hopfield-energy perspectives while retaining linear complexity via FAVOR+/control-variate features, reducing the irreducible error of attention-only ICL under nonzero-mean priors and improving stability on long sequences. We hypothesize gains on nonlinear and shifted-prior ICL benchmarks with minimal compute overhead.

args.text: We propose adversarial policy-ensemble bisimulation (APEB) to address the policy-dependence failures of bisimulation-based representation learning: an encoder is trained to minimize the worst-case bisimulation discrepancy over a learned ensemble of behavior policies and horizons that an adversary optimizes to expose representation collapse. Concretely, we alternate (i) training an adversary that searches over policy mixtures to maximize latent-space deviations in reward and next-embedding predictions, and (ii) updating the encoder so latent distances upper-bound these worst-case deviations, yielding a policy-invariant embedding that transfers off-policy. To stabilize under sparse/delayed rewards, we first pretrain with a predictive-information bottleneck and temporal-contrastive objective, and apply reward-normalized norm constraints before fine-tuning with the adversarial bisimulation loss. APEB should improve robustness to distractors and behavior shifts and can plug into prototype/clustering pipelines and pixel-based RL backbones.

Concretely, video frames are encoded and projected into a volumetric feature grid that a transformer refines through attention-based aggregation across time and views; a coarse-to-fine feature hierarchy is maintained and interpolated to an MLP that predicts surface occupancy for high-resolution implicit reconstruction. This design yields more accurate surface reconstructions than prior multi-view stereo, fully-convolutional volumetric fusion, and recurrent (LSTM/GRU) fusion approaches.

args.text: We propose Policy-Ensemble Bisimulation Embeddings (PEBE): learn state representations by matching successor distributions averaged over a bootstrap ensemble of learned policies, rather than a single (often suboptimal) behavior or the unknown optimal policy. Concretely, a latent world model generates counterfactual rollouts for each ensemble policy to estimate successor features; states whose ensemble successor distributions are close (e.g., Wasserstein distance) are aligned via a contrastive loss, and CBM-style prototypes discretize abstract states for control. Averaging over policy hypotheses mitigates bisimulation pathologies under non-optimal policies and sparse rewards while approximating the PSM intuition without requiring optimal policies. This yields robust, control-sufficient abstractions that improve generalization and stability in visual RL with distractions and distribution shift.

args.text: We propose a diffusion-based reasoner for multi-hop knowledge graphs that generates sequences of relations/entities conditioned on a first-order logic query, using a probabilistic evaluator to guide sampling. Specifically, we use BetaE’s distributional query semantics to provide a differentiable guidance signal for conjunction, disjunction, and negation satisfaction during diffusion sampling, while incorporating GaussianPath-style uncertainty to encourage exploration of ambiguous regions and avoid premature exploitation. We further adopt an AdaptDiffuser-style self-evolving loop that iteratively generates candidate reasoning paths, filters them by BetaE-evaluated query likelihood and diversity, and finetunes the model, progressively improving path quality and coverage. args.text: We propose Uncertainty-Routed Query Adaptation for DETR-style unsupervised domain adaptation, which estimates per-query classification and localization uncertainty from an EMA teacher and routes each object query either to self-training or to masked, query-conditioned feature alignment. Low-uncertainty queries emit pseudo boxes for the student, while high-uncertainty queries bypass pseudo-labeling and instead drive masked discriminators on query/key features and tiled regions to avoid aligning unreliable signals; mid-uncertainty queries are trained with residual-dictionary-derived quality weights to calibrate their localization contribution. Concretely, we obtain per-query uncertainty via Monte Carlo teacher sampling with uncertainty-weighted losses, preserve object-query knowledge transfer during training, and plug a category dictionary module into the box head to compute reconstruction residuals as soft localization quality. This unified routing stabilizes DETR adaptation, improves calibration, and yields stronger target-domain AP than mean-teacher plus masked-alignment baselines.

I propose Region-Conditioned Prototype Prompting (RCPP): use off-the-shelf segmentation masks to partition tokens into foreground and context, compute region-specific token prototypes on downstream data, and initialize two small prompt banks from these prototypes—foreground prompts injected in early layers to modulate masked patches and context prompts injected in mid/late layers to capture background priors (building on prototype-based initialization).
